events.title: A terminal, still on
events.text: The terminal has been left on. A single line blinks on the black: LAST MESSAGE, UNSENT. The keyboard is clean except for three keys, which are worn to the plastic. Whoever sat here wrote this, deleted it, and wrote it again many times before they went. The cursor beats like a pulse.

outcomes.text: It is a handover note, and it is kind. Where the lights are on a timer, which is wrong. How to jiggle the door. Which pipe knocks. At the bottom, small: I'm going to check the pipes now. You copy it to your slate, because it seems wrong for nobody to have it.
The board comes away with a sound like a small sigh. Inside there is a good deal of silicon and a great deal of dust. The cursor blinks once more, out of habit, and goes dark.

The board comes away with a sound like a small sigh, and with it a maintenance cartridge no bigger than a thumb, still warm: the station's own fabricator library. It bites the hand that frees it. The cartridge holds the diagrams of an Assembly Rig, and the cursor, at last, goes out.
It seems kinder.

events.title: Form 22
events.text: A Concord terminal, still logged in under a clerk's name and a half-finished form: FORM 22, REQUEST FOR PERMISSION TO LEAVE. The field headed REASON has been filled in, deleted and filled in again. The last attempt reads simply: BECAUSE. A queue number hangs at the top of the screen. It says you are 1. 'You are being served,' the machine says. Nothing happens.

outcomes.text: You fill in the form, in the clerk's name, and attach the reason. The terminal thinks about it, and then, with something like relief, a stamp comes down on the screen: APPROVED. A drawer somewhere pops open. It holds a small, orderly sum of petty cash.

choices.text: Look for what the clerk was hiding.

outcomes.text: The terminal gives up its secrets without a fight: a locker code, a note, an inventory. 'ITEM 4,112: VESSEL, UNIDENTIFIED (PROVISIONAL),' it says of you, with some warmth.
An alarm the clerk never meant to arm goes off, three decks down. Something that was asleep wakes up in a very bad mood. 'You have been served,' the terminal says.

The terminal opens a drawer you did not ask for: a technical annex, misfiled under MISCELLANEOUS, the plans for a laser of a finer cut than the clerk's whole department. It sends them to you with a receipt. The same drawer rings a bell three decks down, a short one, and something small and awake starts up the stairs.

choices.text: Leave the queue as it is.

outcomes.text: The number at the top of the screen goes on saying you are 1.

events.title: RB-9
events.text: A relay terminal, tagged RB-9 in white paint, with a tally scratched into its casing that goes up in fives to a number you do not try to read. A speaker the size of a coaster crackles in the wall above it. The screen is a log: a line, forty seconds long, repeated. SIGNAL RECEIVED. SIGNAL RECEIVED. Under that, in pencil taped to the glass: HOAX (RESOLVED). Someone has crossed out HOAX.

outcomes.text: A small tired voice says it. We're alive, it says. Come to the Lantern Reach. A chair scrapes. Somebody coughs. The tally on the casing, you realise, counts times heard, not times believed, and the clerk who kept it stopped counting on the last day and started to listen. You copy the log, and the bearing the relay stamped on its last fix.

The core comes out clean. It is warm, and heavier than it ought to be. When you turn it over the pencil on the glass has gone, like a breath on a mirror, and the speaker has gone quiet. You will have to take it on trust, what it said.
The speaker crackles once, politely, as you go.

events.title: A note in the pocket
events.text: The body is sitting against the wall with one hand on a pocket, as if to keep something in. The suit is a Drift suit, patched, kind to its owner. A scrap of paper is held in the pocket by the corner, between two fingers, deliberately. Nothing else is wrong with the room. That is the part you do not like.

outcomes.text: The fingers let go as though they had been waiting. It is a note, in a neat hand, to someone called Marl: where the card is, which door is not a door, and an apology about the smell. You read it, and then fold it small, and put it somewhere safe.

choices.text: Close the eyes and go through the other pockets.

outcomes.text: You do the first without thinking and the second with a little shame. A few loose credits, a lighter, a photo of a dog on a rocket crate. You leave the photo. You take the rest, and put the dog back where the hand was.
You say something, quietly, that you do not remember afterwards.

events.title: Still warm
events.text: The body on the deck is face down, one arm out, as if reaching for the door. It is wearing a good suit. It is also, you notice in the instant before you take another step, the only thing in this corridor with a clean boot-print leading in. The air at your back is colder than it should be. The corridor is very still.

choices.text: Step over it and keep going.

outcomes.text: You step over. A hand closes on nothing where your ankle was, and something further back makes a long unhappy sound. By the time you look the corridor is empty and the boot-prints lead away. On the belt of the suit is a pouch, still sealed.
Your foot comes down and the body gets up. It is not the body. The body had company, and the company has been waiting for exactly this.

choices.text: Turn the body over and look.

outcomes.text: The face is a stranger's and long past worrying. There is a keycard on a lanyard round the neck, and a tag with a name you do not read.
It is not a stranger's face, quite. It is a face that has been made to look like one. 'Hello,' it says, and the rest of the corridor says it with it.
Nothing follows you. You are almost sure.

events.title: Table for eleven
events.text: The mess room is warm. That is the first thing, and it is wrong: warm air in a dead place. A long table has been laid for a dinner party. You count the chairs before you can stop yourself: eleven, pushed back at the same angle, the way people stand when someone important comes in. Eleven bowls. The steam is still coming off every one. Nobody here, and the soup smells good.

choices.text: Pull up a chair at the end, and eat.

outcomes.text: The chair is there when you reach for it. You eat. The soup is soup. When you put the spoon down every other spoon, up and down the table, goes down with it, once, in time. You say 'Thank you,' not knowing who to. Somewhere, the sound of eleven chairs pushing back to stand. You leave quickly, and a little tucked in.

choices.text: Count the bowls and take notes.

outcomes.text: You write down what you see, and it reads, in your own hand, like a thing a person would write in a calm and ordinary place. Eleven bowls. Eleven chairs. One note on the wall, in a clean hand: WE'RE SO GLAD YOU CAME. You take the paper down and fold it away.

It is very good silver. It is also still warm, and by the time you reach the door it is a little warmer. You leave it on the sill. It follows you with its eyes, in the way spoons do. You keep the one you did not mean to take.

choices.text: Leave the table as it is.

outcomes.text: The steam goes on, from eleven bowls, without a draught.

events.title: The quiet room
events.text: Your boots stop making a sound at the door. It is not that the room is silent: it is that the sound stops at the threshold, like a coat handed in. You can see your torch beam, and your breath, and nothing else. In the middle of the floor someone has drawn a circle in chalk and set a single chair in it, facing the wall.

choices.text: Step in and sit in the chair.

outcomes.text: You sit. The quiet closes round you like water, and your shoulders come down for the first time in days. Time goes strange. When you stand, the world's noises come back all at once, and your hands are steady. You feel, in some way you cannot name, forgiven.

You sit. The quiet is not empty. In it, very clearly, someone says your name, in a voice you almost knew. You are on your feet and in the corridor before you decide to move. Your heart goes for ten minutes.

choices.text: Toss a bolt in, and back out.

outcomes.text: The bolt goes in without a sound and stays where it lands. Another, a heartbeat later, lands beside it. Neither of you threw it. You step back, carefully, as one steps back from a drop.

events.title: The wake
events.text: A hall set for a wake, with the benches pushed in two long rows and a keg on a trestle at the head. A banner over it, in the clan's lopsided hand: TUSK, OWED EVERYONE. Somebody has left a mug on the keg lid, half full, and a plate under a cloth. There is a coat over the back of the head chair, and a hat on the coat, and the hat is not quite straight.

outcomes.text: You drink, and it is dreadful, and you do it properly anyway, for the length of one very slow breath. Something in the room eases. A slip of paper under the mug is the menu, in somebody's blocky hand. You pocket it, and the name.

The keg is mostly sediment, and one very large final bottle in a straw jacket, hidden in the false bottom by a person who knew exactly who would come looking. It is worth a good deal to the right buyer, and a good deal of grief to the wrong one.
You straighten it. The hall seems to take a breath. A voice, in the dark, deep and unhurried, says 'Cheers,' and does not need an answer.
The mug stays where it was. So does the hat.

events.title: Bunks, made
events.text: Twelve bunks in two rows, every one made with hospital corners, every pillow squared. Dust lies on them in a single even layer, like a second blanket. Only the lowest bunk by the door has been slept in, and recently: the cover is thrown back and a boot has been left under it, laces still tied.

choices.text: Check the bag under the slept-in bunk.

outcomes.text: A kit bag, packed to go and never carried. Rounds for a small weapon, a folded credit chit, a tin of boot polish that has outlived its owner.
Clothes, a toothbrush, and a room card pinned inside the lining with a safety pin. The card is for a door two rooms down. Whoever packed this meant to leave.

You straighten the cover and square the pillow. It takes ten seconds and feels like signing something. On the wall above the head someone has scratched a tally, and under it a list of where the spare tanks went.

choices.text: Close the door on the room as you found it.

outcomes.text: The latch clicks. Behind it the bunks go on being tidier than your ship has ever been.

events.title: One note
events.text: A pressure line runs along the ceiling and has split at a flange. It lets out a thin, steady whistle from a pinhole that has been taped twice and then given up on. The grating beneath the leak is slick, and the locker you want is on the far side of it.

outcomes.text: The valve is stiff and goes on a count of nine. The whistle winds down like a tired kettle. The locker behind it opens without argument and holds a few spare parts.

choices.text: Cross the grating at a run.

outcomes.text: Four steps, and the pinhole misses you by a hand. The locker is full of fittings and a sealed pack of rounds.
The line coughs as you pass and the jet takes the skin off a forearm. You get the locker open one-handed and take what the other hand can hold.

choices.text: Follow the pipe to see where it goes.

outcomes.text: It runs through two walls and ends at a junction stencilled SPARES, ROOM 3. Somebody has chalked an arrow on the floor to match.

choices.text: Back out and let it sing.

outcomes.text: You pull the door to on the whistle. It carries on, one note, to an empty room.

events.title: Eighty seconds
events.text: A hatch in the far wall with a keypad and a red countdown, frozen at 01:20. A strip of tape beside it reads, in marker, ONCE IT STARTS YOU CANNOT STOP IT. Under that, in a different marker: it's fine, I did it, just be patient. One key on the pad is worn through to the plastic.

choices.text: Press the key and wait it out.

outcomes.text: The count begins. Eighty seconds is a long time in a room you do not know. Nothing comes. At zero the bolts draw back with a satisfied thump, and behind the hatch is a stack of crates somebody was proud of.
The count begins. At about forty seconds something that heard the keypad beep comes to see what it is for. The hatch opens on schedule regardless, which is something.
The bar goes in and you lean. The hatch gives with a crack that goes up your arms, and inside there is only what is easy to grab.
You note the hatch, the tape and the two different markers, and carry on. Some doors want your hands free. Your map keeps the spot.
The tape's promise follows you down the corridor. It is probably true.

events.title: Outlines
events.text: A workshop wall with a painted outline for every tool: a hammer here, a cutter there, a torque wrench the size of a forearm. Almost every outline is empty, stained with the dust the tools left behind. One hook still holds its tool, and a roster is pinned under the board with a column for who signed what out.

choices.text: Take the tool on the hook.

outcomes.text: A pry bar, heavy and honest, with a name scratched in the handle. Taking it leaves a gap you find you do not like. The board looks, suddenly, less finished.

Down the column, in six different hands, the same names, and then fewer names. The last line is a torque wrench signed out by someone who wrote back by end of shift in the box marked date. You copy the sheet.

choices.text: Hang a spare on an empty outline.

outcomes.text: It fits no outline, but the board looks better for it. Behind the board a panel you had not noticed swings out an inch, on a tin of fittings somebody saved for exactly this.
The empty outlines watch you go, patient as stencils.

events.title: The plate that moves
events.text: One floor plate in this room sits a finger higher than its neighbours, and the scratches round its edge are fresh, bright metal against old grey. Someone has been lifting it, often, with a blade. A stool stands beside it, set where you would sit to watch.

outcomes.text: Under the plate, in a hollow cut for the purpose, is a roll of cloth with a few rounds and a purse of credits. The scratches stop making sense and then make exactly the right sense.
The hollow is empty except for a folded note: IT WAS EMPTY BEFORE YOU. SORRY. A small drawing of a face. You laugh, which helps.
A wire trips as the plate rises and a spark jumps your knuckles. The hollow holds the wire and two spent rounds.

choices.text: Slide a blade under the edge first.

outcomes.text: The blade finds a wire. You cut it, then lift the plate with care. The hollow holds a roll of cloth with a few rounds and a purse.

choices.text: Sit on the stool and watch the room.

outcomes.text: From the stool you can see every way in, and after a while the thing the watcher was watching for: a hairline of light under the far door, where somebody left a lamp on. You know where to look next.

choices.text: Set the stool straight and go.

outcomes.text: You nudge the stool back to where it was. Whoever owns the plate will know someone looked, and you hope they are all right.

events.title: Ankle deep
events.text: A foot of still water covers this room from wall to wall, black and level, with a skin of old lamp oil that breaks into colours when you step in. Lockers line the far wall at waist height. The top one is propped open with a boot, the way you prop a door when you mean to come back.

choices.text: Wade over and open the top locker.

outcomes.text: The water is colder than it looks and the locker drier than it should be. A keycard on a lanyard, a flask, a sheet of instructions for a door.
Halfway there a cable you cannot see takes your ankle, and the water remembers it is a conductor. You reach the locker anyway. You get back less pleased.
It is on the wall beside the door, under a hand-lettered label: DON'T. You do. The room ticks as it discharges, and the water is only water. The top locker holds a keycard on a lanyard and a flask.

choices.text: Pull the boot out of the doorway and go.

outcomes.text: A good boot, left foot, size eleven. You shake the water out of it and put it back where it was. You could not say why.

events.title: On shift
events.text: A man sits in the chair at the main console with his hands in his lap and his head tipped back, as if he stopped to think. A mug stands at his elbow. The console is awake on one window, the cursor in the middle of a sentence, and the card on the lanyard round his neck is the cleanest thing in the room.

choices.text: Take the card from his neck.

outcomes.text: The lanyard lifts over his head more easily than it should. The card is stamped for a door on this deck. Under his hand, where it hung, is a pencilled scrap: sorry, needed that.

It is the handover to the next shift, and a good one. Pump three sounds worse than it is. The coffee is in the second drawer. If anything strange happens, do nothing heroic and call the number on the wall. The number on the wall is his own. You save the page.

choices.text: Turn his chair to the window.

outcomes.text: It rolls without a sound. Outside the glass is only the black and your own reflection, which is not the worst company he could have had. You leave the mug where it was, and feel steadier for it.
You step back from the console. In the lamplight he looks like a man who had it all in hand.

events.title: Under the blanket
events.text: A body under a grey blanket, tucked at the edges, lying on a cargo pallet with its feet toward the door. Somebody weighted the corners with four tins. A scrawl on the nearest crate reads SORRY, WE HAD TO GO, and below it, in another hand, WE'LL BE BACK FOR YOU.

outcomes.text: Lamp fuel, not rations, whatever the labels say in their hurry. You thank the pallet aloud, which feels odd and also correct.
A woman in a good coat, very still. One hand holds a pass key against her chest, carefully, as if she had been asked to mind it. You take it with a nod to her.
No one. A coil of cable, a rolled mat, and the shape of a person made with great care by somebody who wanted a door left alone. Under the mat, a hatch.
You square the edges and set the tins back on their corners. The writing on the crate looks less lonely with something holding it down.

events.title: Vending, still hopeful
events.text: A vending console in an alcove, its screen cycling through the same three products with the prices struck out and rewritten in grease pencil. A strip of tape covers the coin slot, and a note: JUST PRESS THE BUTTON. THE BUTTON IS FREE. THE MACHINE KNOWS.

outcomes.text: A tray drops. A sealed pack of rounds, a decade past its use-by date, with a sticker: ENJOY.
A tray drops. A clatter, a tin of something, a coil of cable. The screen says THANK YOU in four languages.
The machine hiccups, rattles, and shrieks a three-note jingle from every speaker on the deck. It has never been so pleased to see anyone.
The jingle dies at the first note. The tray drops anyway, on spring pressure alone, with a clunk and a pack of rounds.
The last technician was thorough. The log lists which crates on this deck were restocked, in order, and the order is a map.
The screen thanks you, in four languages, for a loyalty it has no way to check.

events.title: Who went through
events.text: A door controller with a screen the size of a hand, still logging. It lists the last forty openings of the hatch beside it: time, card number, direction. The entries are regular for a long stretch, in and out, in and out, and then they are all in. The last is a card number and the word IN, with no word after it.

choices.text: Match the card numbers to names.

outcomes.text: The controller keeps a name for each card, in a small embarrassed font. Twelve names, then nine, then four. The last card belongs to an Odette, who typed her own name in the notes field in capitals, in case anyone should ever need it. You copy the list.

choices.text: Open the hatch with that last card number.

outcomes.text: The controller considers it, then agrees. Somewhere on the deck a lock you could not read clicks, and your map marks it.
The controller takes a note. You type HERE, and after a pause, THANKS. It files both, under IN.
